# 04 Lexus ES330 Multiple Ignition Coil Failures / Poor Coil Feedback Signal

When a Lexus ES330 refuses to exceed 20 MPH and drops into limp mode immediately after startup, standard ECM replacement procedures often fail to resolve the issue. In this specific case, the engine control module had already been swapped, yet the vehicle continued to hit fuel cut conditions. The diagnostic trouble codes (DTCs) pointed clearly at the ignition system: P0351 through P0356, indicating cylinder misfires for all six firing coils. These codes set instantly upon cranking, suggesting a fundamental communication breakdown rather than a random misfire caused by fouled plugs or worn spark plug wires.

To isolate the fault, we moved beyond visual inspection and utilized an oscilloscope to capture the ignition timing signals. By inserting a wire loop into the IGN fuse, we could monitor the Ignition Timing (IGT) signal sent from the Engine Control Module (ECM) alongside the primary coil output. The initial parade pattern showed the IGT signal (yellow trace) triggering correctly across all cylinders. Furthermore, using an adjustable spark tester confirmed that secondary voltage was present at the plugs. This ruled out a complete loss of primary power as the root cause; the system was attempting to fire, but something was interrupting the process prematurely.

Zooming out on the scope capture reveals the critical failure mode: the ECM stops commanding fuel injection precisely when it detects a fault in the ignition feedback loop. The engine is effectively choking itself because the control logic interprets the missing feedback as a catastrophic misfire, triggering an immediate fuel cut to prevent potential damage.

On Toyota and Lexus platforms, the ignition system operates on a sophisticated request-feedback protocol. The ECM outputs a high-side driver signal (IGT) to activate the coil ignitor. In response, the ignitor must generate a low-side ground pulse back to the PCM via the Ignition Feedback (IGF) terminal. This IGF pulse confirms that the primary current has been switched off and the secondary spark has occurred. The oscilloscope parade pattern captures these synchronized events for all six coils simultaneously.

However, in this scenario, the feedback loop was compromised. By back-probing terminal 24 on the E10 connector at the PCM against the #6 IGF terminal, we observed a distinct lack of return signal from the ignitors. The waveform showed either significant noise superimposed on the IGT ramp-up or a complete absence of the expected IGF pulse. Without this confirmation signal, the ECM cannot verify that combustion is occurring as intended, leading to the immediate fault detection and fuel cut logic.

The central diagnostic challenge arises here: why would all six ignitors fail simultaneously? Common theories often blame a power surge from an alternator spike or a failing internal driver within the PCM itself. While these are plausible failure modes for modern electronics, they are less common on platforms with older ignition architectures like the ES330.

To determine the root cause without immediately replacing expensive components, a targeted resistance and isolation test is required. The technician should measure the primary coil resistance on each of the six coils to ensure they match manufacturer specifications exactly. If the resistances are uniform, the next step involves isolating the ECM drivers from the external circuit. By disconnecting the harness connectors at the ignition control module (ICM) or direct injector-coil pack and applying a known good ground directly to the IGF terminals using an external power supply, one can verify if the ECM drivers themselves are capable of switching without load.

If the external test reveals that the PCM drivers function correctly but fail when connected to the vehicle harness, the issue likely lies within the harness wiring, specifically looking for high resistance connections or poor crimps at the coil connectors. Conversely, if the external test fails to trigger the IGF pulse despite a healthy ground, it points toward an internal failure of the PCM driver stage. Given that multiple coils are involved, a shared power or ground fault in the harness is a strong candidate before assuming a mass failure of the ignitor chips themselves.

Accurate diagnosis here requires patience and precise signal analysis rather than part swapping. Relying solely on code scanning can lead to unnecessary ECM replacements, as the PCM may be functioning perfectly while misinterpreting noisy or absent feedback signals from a compromised harness connection.
